selected.hypothesis: Electrides can be distinguished by (i) lack of a neutral oxidation‑state assignment, (ii) presence of strongly electro‑positive cations (low min electronegativity, high alkali/alkaline fraction), and (iii) large interstitial voids (high max clearance and positive mean clearance).

final_fit.note: Model fitted on all labeled structures; probability >= 0.5 means electride. Missing feature values are imputed with the median of these structures.

leaderboard.hypothesis: Electrides can be distinguished by (i) lack of a neutral oxidation‑state assignment, (ii) presence of strongly electro‑positive cations (low min electronegativity, high alkali/alkaline fraction), and (iii) large interstitial voids (high max clearance and positive mean clearance).

Electrides are characterized by (1) a large individual interstitial cavity, (2) overall lattice openness (average clearance), (3) a rich network of viable void sites, and (4) a strongly electropositive chemical environment (high alkali/alkaline‑earth fraction and low minimum electronegativity).

Electrides are identified by (1) a large individual interstitial cavity, (2) overall spacious lattice (high per‑atom volume and average cavity clearance), (3) a chemical environment rich in electropositive elements (high alkali/alkaline‑earth fraction and low minimum electronegativity), which together enable excess electrons to reside in interstitial sites.

Electrides are identified by (1) a very large interstitial cavity, (2) an overall open lattice (high volume per atom), (3) a rich network of viable void sites, and (4‑5) a strongly electropositive chemical environment (high alkali/alkaline‑earth fraction and low minimum electronegativity).

Electrides can be identified by (1) a very large interstitial cavity, (2) an even larger sampled clearance indicating extreme openness, (3) a high count of viable void‑center candidates reflecting a rich interstitial network, (4) a chemical environment rich in electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth elements, and (5) a very low minimum Pauling electronegativity, together enabling excess electrons to reside in the lattice.

Electrides are characterised by (1) a very large interstitial cavity, (2) a heterogeneous void landscape indicating isolated spacious sites, (3) a high number of geometrically viable void candidates, and (4‑5) a strongly electropositive chemical environment (high alkali/alkaline‑earth fraction and low minimum electronegativity).

Electrides are distinguished by (1) large and heterogeneous interstitial voids, (2) a strongly electropositive chemical environment, and (3) a quantitative excess‑electron signature reflected in many plausible oxidation‑state assignments.

Electrides are characterized by a high proportion of electropositive alkali/alkaline‑earth cations, low minimum Pauling electronegativity, large interstitial voids, and an excess of valence electrons that prevents a neutral oxidation‑state assignment.
